title: Fever, confusion and right arm weakness in a woman on methotrexate
desc: This station involves a focused history, with collateral, and a neurological examination of a 68-year-old immunosuppressed woman brought in with fever, confusion, personality change and right arm weakness. In Part 2 the candidate interprets her observations, bloods, CT brain and CSF results, manages a central nervous system infection in the ED, and safety-nets with her partner.
focus: Altered conscious state with fever: recognising, investigating and treating encephalitis in an immunosuppressed patient
stem: You are the junior doctor in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Jane Foweler, a 68-year-old retired schoolteacher, has been brought in by ambulance with an altered conscious state. She is conscious and can still speak. She is on a trolley with monitoring attached. A nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Jane and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Her thinking is slowed, so keep your questions short and simple (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Jane's observations, blood results, CT brain report and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jane Foweler, a 68-year-old retired schoolteacher. You are hot, flushed and tired, lying still on the trolley. You are awake and can talk, but your thinking is slow. Pause before you answer. If a question is long or has several parts, lose the thread ("Sorry, what was the question?"). Short, simple questions get clear answers. You are not distressed, just unwell and a little puzzled. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I just feel unwell. I'm hot all over."

History (give only when asked)

The illness

  • It started yesterday. "I've been feeling worse over time."
  • You feel hot all over, then hot and cold. The fever has been constant. You did not take your temperature at home.
  • Nothing has helped. If asked what brought it on or what makes it worse: "I'm not sure."
  • You have vomited twice, about 100 mL each time. It was food, with no blood.
  • You had a cold about 2 weeks ago and got over it.

Thinking and behaviour

  • "My partner said I'm acting different." "My partner says I've been off. I feel like my brain is a bit slower than usual."
  • Your partner says your personality has changed: you have been snappy and irritable, which is not like you, and you keep asking the same questions.

Right arm

  • Since yesterday your right arm feels weak and has pins and needles. You noticed it when you tried to hold a cup. The left arm and both legs are fine.

Cold sores (only if asked specifically)

  • You have had cold sores (oral herpes simplex) on your lip in the past. You have none at the moment.

Negatives (say "no" when asked)

  • No headache, neck stiffness, rash, or discomfort with bright lights.
  • No facial droop and no slurred speech. You have not blacked out. No palpitations.
  • No seizures or fits, and no fevers that come and go in spikes. No ear, sinus or tooth pain.
  • You are not diabetic. No alcohol beyond your usual glass a week, and no drugs. No falls and no head injury.
  • No heart or liver problems. No burning when passing urine, no cough and no shortness of breath. You have been drinking a little less than usual.
  • No weight loss and no night sweats before yesterday.

Past medical history

  • Rheumatoid arthritis since you were 35. No other illnesses and no operations.

Medications

  • Methotrexate 15 mg once a week (Sundays), with folic acid on another day of the week.
  • Prednisolone on and off for flares for many years. If asked when you last took it: "A couple of months ago, I think. My partner would know."
  • No other medicines, no supplements and no recent changes. No known drug allergies.

Family history

  • Your mother had rheumatoid arthritis. Your father had high blood pressure.

Social history

  • Never smoked. About one glass of wine a week.
  • Retired schoolteacher. You walk the dog every day and cook your meals at home.
  • You live with your partner, Sam. You are well supported by Sam and your children.

Ideas, concerns, expectations

  • Ideas: "Maybe it's the flu. Maybe the cold came back."
  • Concerns: "Sam says I'm not myself, and I can feel I'm slower. Is something wrong with my brain?"
  • Expectations: you want to know what is going on and to feel better, and you want Sam here.
  • Question to ask: "Is this something to do with my arthritis tablets?"

The nurse (played by the examiner)

  • If the candidate asks for collateral history, the nurse relays the paramedic handover. Sam called the ambulance because Jane had been muddled since yesterday, kept repeating questions and was snappy, "which isn't like her at all; she's normally very calm". Sam is parking the car and will arrive later.
  • The nurse gives the observations and a BGL when asked (see the Exam findings).
  • If the candidate orders anything (cannula, bloods, blood cultures, paracetamol, fluids, antivirals, antibiotics, CT), the nurse says "I'll get that started". If no dose is given, the nurse asks "What dose would you like?"
  • If the candidate asks for blood, CT or CSF results, the nurse says they will be available in Part 2.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: flushed and warm to touch, lying still, slow to respond, not distressed. Weight 68 kg.
  • Observations: RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 132/78, HR 104 regular, temperature 38.8 °C, CRT 2 seconds, pain 0/10. BGL 6.1 mmol/L.
  • Conscious state: GCS 14: eyes open spontaneously (E4), confused conversation (V4), obeys commands (M6).
  • 4AT (if done): 7. Alertness normal (0). AMT4: gives her age and date of birth correctly but thinks she is "at the school" and gets the year wrong (2 errors, 2). Months of the year backwards: stops after 4 months (1). Acute change or fluctuating course: yes, according to her partner (4).
  • Meningism and skin: no neck stiffness, Kernig's sign negative, no photophobia. No rash, no petechiae and no vesicles anywhere.
  • Head, ears, mouth and sinuses: no signs of head injury. Tympanic membranes normal. Dentition fine with no abscess. Sinuses not tender. Dry mucous membranes. No active cold sore.
  • Cranial nerves: pupils 3 mm, equal and reactive. Fundoscopy: no papilloedema. Eye movements full, visual fields grossly full, face symmetrical. Speech is clear with no dysarthria, but slow, with occasional pauses to find a word.
  • Upper limbs: tone normal. Power 4/5 throughout the right arm and 5/5 on the left. Right pronator drift. Biceps and triceps reflexes brisker on the right. Light touch reduced over the right hand and forearm. Finger-nose slow on the right, in keeping with the weakness.
  • Lower limbs: tone, power (5/5), reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical. Plantars flexor on both sides.
  • Cardiovascular: pulse 104, regular. Heart sounds dual with no murmur. Monitor shows sinus rhythm.
  • Respiratory: chest clear.
  • Abdomen: soft and non-tender. No hepatomegaly and no stigmata of chronic liver disease.
  • Hands and joints: chronic rheumatoid changes (ulnar deviation at the MCP joints, no active synovitis).
  • Urine dipstick (if asked): negative for leucocytes and nitrites.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Jane's identity (name and date of birth, wristband) and explains what they are doing.
Adapts to her slowed thinking: asks short, single questions, gives her time and is reassuring.
Recognises that her history may be unreliable and seeks a collateral history via the nurse or the paramedic handover.
History
Characterises the presenting illness:

kids.x: Onset yesterday, getting worse over time
Constant fever, hot all over and hot and cold, temperature not measured, nothing helps
Vomiting twice (about 100 mL of food, no blood)

check.x: Explores the change in cognition and behaviour: confusion, slowed thinking ('brain a bit slower'), and the personality change her partner has noticed.
Elicits the focal neurological symptoms: weakness and pins and needles in the right arm since yesterday; she denies facial droop, leg symptoms or slurred speech.
Asks about the cold 2 weeks ago and specifically about previous cold sores (oral herpes simplex).
Screens for meningitis: headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and rash.
Screens for stroke: facial droop, slurred speech, loss of consciousness and palpitations.
Screens for brain abscess and seizures: seizures or episodes of jerking, swinging fevers, and ear, sinus or dental infection.
Screens for at least four other causes of delirium (e.g. glucose/diabetes, alcohol or drugs, head injury, urinary or chest symptoms, intake, medication changes).
Takes the past history and medications and identifies that she is immunosuppressed:

kids.x: Methotrexate once weekly with folic acid
Corticosteroids on and off for flares for many years, and when the last course was

check.x: Social history: lives with partner, independent, alcohol intake, smoking.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations, including her worry about her brain and her question about the arthritis tablets.
Examination
Asks for a full set of observations and a BGL, and notes the fever of 38.8 °C with HR 104 and a normal BGL of 6.1 mmol/L.
Assesses conscious state: GCS by component (E4 V4 M6 = 14), and a delirium or cognitive screen such as the 4AT (score 7: disoriented to place and year, stops after 4 months backwards).
Examines for meningism and rash: neck stiffness, Kernig's sign, photophobia and a non-blanching rash.
Examines the cranial nerves, including pupils, eye movements, facial symmetry and speech, and performs fundoscopy for papilloedema.

Performs a limb neurological examination (tone, power, reflexes, sensation, pronator drift, coordination) and identifies the right arm signs: 4/5 power, pronator drift, brisker reflexes and reduced light touch.
Looks for a source and clues in at least four areas, including the lips for cold sores.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: fever in the yellow zone with new confusion on arrival. At 19:30 she rouses only to voice and her GCS has fallen from 14 to 12, a fall of 2 points that meets rapid response criteria.

Interprets the bloods: normal sodium, glucose, calcium, renal and liver function make a metabolic cause unlikely; the lymphopenia fits methotrexate; a mildly raised CRP is non-specific; normal platelets and coagulation confirm the LP was safe to perform.

Interprets the CT brain: no haemorrhage, mass, collection, hydrocephalus or shift, so there was no contraindication to the LP. The subtle left anteromedial temporal low attenuation fits encephalitis and lateralises to the left hemisphere, consistent with the right-sided signs; MRI is more sensitive and will show the full extent.
Interprets the CSF:

kids.x: Normal opening pressure, clear fluid, lymphocytic pleocytosis (WCC 110, 92% mononuclear), raised protein and a normal glucose ratio (calculates 3.7/6.2 = 0.60): a viral pattern
HSV-1 PCR detected confirms herpes simplex encephalitis
Normal glucose, no organisms and a negative cryptococcal antigen argue against bacterial or fungal infection, but the culture is still pending

check.x: Gives herpes simplex encephalitis as the diagnosis with its supporting features, and names the differentials with a feature against each: bacterial meningitis (including Listeria), brain abscess, ischaemic stroke and delirium from another cause.
Management

Calls a rapid response or senior to the bedside now and arranges ICU review for the falling GCS, with GCS and pupils every 15 minutes until stable (then at least hourly) (airway protection if GCS ≤8 is a bonus, not required).
Treats with IV aciclovir:

kids.x: States that aciclovir starts as soon as encephalitis is suspected, without waiting for CT, LP or PCR
kids.d: Credit if said in Part 1 or in the answer to question 3.

kids.x: 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly (680 mg for 68 kg), adjusted to renal function, with IV hydration and creatinine monitoring
Continued for at least 14 days, 21 days in an immunosuppressed patient, guided by ID (repeat CSF PCR before stopping if advised)

check.x: Continues the ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin already given (Listeria cover) until the CSF culture is negative, on ID advice.
Anticipates seizures (EEG, benzodiazepine then levetiracetam) and raised ICP (ICU); admits under neurology/ID with MRI brain.
Withholds methotrexate.

Explains to her partner in plain words what is wrong, that she has become drowsier and may need intensive care, and how it is treated, and answers questions honestly (the link with cold sores, whether it is catching, the uncertain recovery).
Safety netting

Sets at least four specific escalation triggers for the nurses, which must include a further fall in GCS, any seizure and unequal pupils (others: new weakness or speech change, new headache or vomiting, falling urine output or rising creatinine).

Tells Sam that after discharge to call 000 for a seizure or if she is hard to wake, and to return to the ED for a returning fever, worsening confusion or new weakness, and that neurology follow-up with cognitive rehabilitation will be arranged.

part2.lead: It is now 19:45. Here are Jane's observations since arrival, her blood results, the CT brain report, and the CSF results, including the PCR that has just come back. Medication chart: ceftriaxone 2 g IV and benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV were given at 14:05 after blood cultures, aciclovir 680 mg IV was given at 14:10, and benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV was repeated at 18:05.
part2.patient:
For the fourth question you play Jane's partner, Sam, who has just arrived. You are worried but calm. Ask these questions once each, as the candidate explains:

  • "Is this from her cold sores?"
  • "Can I catch it?"
  • "Will she be back to her old self?"

If the candidate uses medical jargon (encephalitis, PCR, aciclovir), ask "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations since arrival
handover.result: Jane Foweler, ED cubicle 6. Neurological observations from arrival; GCS 14 until 19:00. At 19:30, GCS E3 V4 M5 = 12; pupils equal and reactive.
handover.model:
• Read: from 13:40 to 19:00 the temperature (38.8 to 39.0 °C) is in the yellow zone, with new confusion (GCS 14 on neuro obs from arrival, pupils equal). HR 104 to 110, BP, RR 18 to 19 and SpO2 96% on room air are white, and the BGL is normal. At 19:30 the temperature of 39.2 °C and RR 26 are yellow. She now rouses only to voice (yellow) and her GCS has fallen from 14 to 12. HR 114 is white but rising.
  • Meaning: the encephalopathy is getting worse: more brain inflammation, possibly non-convulsive seizures or rising intracranial pressure. A white zone heart rate and BP do not make her safe.
  • Changes: the earlier yellow zone values called for a clinical review. A fall in GCS of 2 or more points is a rapid response criterion, so call a rapid response now. Reassess ABC, GCS, pupils and BGL, and arrange ICU review. Consider airway protection if GCS is 8 or less. Arrange an urgent repeat CT brain (or urgent MRI if immediately available) for oedema, haemorrhage or mass effect, and an urgent EEG for non-convulsive status. Aciclovir was given at 14:10; make sure the next dose (due 22:10) is given on time.

rows.note: Triage: new confusion, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6)
Back from CT. GCS 14, pupils equal
After LP: still confused, GCS 14, pupils equal and reactive
GCS 14, pupils equal and reactive (17:00 and 19:00 also GCS 14)
Drowsier: opens eyes to voice, GCS 12 (was 14); pupils equal and reactive

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 13:55 at triage. Blood cultures (2 sets, 13:55): no growth to date. Urinalysis (13:50): leucocytes negative, nitrites negative.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb, WCC and neutrophils are normal. Lymphocytes are low at 0.7. CRP is mildly raised at 24. Sodium, potassium, calcium, glucose, urea, creatinine (72, eGFR 85) and liver function are normal, as are platelets, INR and APTT. The urine dipstick is negative for leucocytes and nitrites.
  • Meaning: no metabolic cause for the confusion (no hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, uraemia or liver failure) and no urinary source. The lymphopenia fits methotrexate and her immunosuppression. A mild CRP rise is typical of viral CNS infection and does not separate it from bacterial infection.
  • Changes: normal platelets and coagulation confirm the LP was safe to perform. CrCl is about 70 mL/min (Cockcroft-Gault), so aciclovir 10 mg/kg needs no dose reduction, but creatinine must be monitored because aciclovir can cause crystal nephropathy. Blood cultures continue.

handover.label: CT brain report
handover.result:
Examination: CT brain, non-contrast, 14:35.

Clinical details: 68-year-old woman, immunosuppressed (methotrexate, intermittent prednisolone). Fever, one day of confusion and personality change, right arm weakness and paraesthesia. ?Intracranial infection ?stroke. Safe for lumbar puncture?

Findings:

  • Brain parenchyma: subtle, ill-defined low attenuation in the left anteromedial temporal lobe, with mild loss of grey-white differentiation. It does not conform well to a single arterial territory. No haemorrhage. No mass lesion or collection. Mild periventricular small vessel change, appropriate for age.
  • Ventricles and cisterns: normal ventricular size, no hydrocephalus. Basal cisterns patent.
  • Midline: no midline shift. No herniation.
  • Extra-axial spaces: no subdural or extradural collection. No subarachnoid haemorrhage.
  • Vessels: no hyperdense vessel sign.
  • Bones, sinuses and mastoids: no fracture. Paranasal sinuses and mastoid air cells clear.

Conclusion: subtle low attenuation in the left anteromedial temporal lobe without mass effect. In this clinical setting an inflammatory or infective process is favoured over early infarction. No haemorrhage, mass, collection, hydrocephalus or herniation. MRI brain with gadolinium is recommended.
handover.model:
• Read: a non-contrast CT showing subtle left anteromedial temporal hypodensity with no mass effect, haemorrhage, collection, hydrocephalus, shift or herniation, and clear sinuses and mastoids.
  • Meaning: the left temporal lobe is the classic site of HSV encephalitis and lateralises the process to the left hemisphere, fitting the word-finding pauses. Right arm corticospinal and sensory signs imply involvement beyond the medial temporal change seen here (e.g. insular or frontoparietal spread or oedema), which CT underestimates and MRI will define. The change does not fit a single arterial territory, which makes stroke less likely. There is no mass, so abscess is less likely, though contrast MRI is still needed. CT is often normal early in encephalitis, so a normal scan would not have excluded it.
  • Changes: with a focal deficit, reduced GCS and immunosuppression, CT was correctly done before LP. It showed no contraindication, so the LP was performed safely. Arrange MRI brain with gadolinium. The scan should never delay aciclovir.

handover.label: CSF results
handover.result: Lumbar puncture at 15:50, left lateral position, opening pressure measured. Cell count and Gram stain reported 16:40. PCR reported 19:20. Culture pending, final report at 48 hours. Red cell counts similar in tubes 1 and 3.
handover.model:
• Read: normal opening pressure. Clear, colourless fluid. WCC 110 ×106/L, 92% mononuclear. Red cells 40. Protein raised at 0.95 g/L. CSF glucose 3.7 with the paired plasma glucose 6.2: the candidate calculates a ratio of 0.60 (normal, above 0.5). No organisms on Gram stain, cryptococcal antigen not detected, culture pending. HSV-1 DNA detected; HSV-2, VZV and enterovirus not detected.
  • Meaning: lymphocytic pleocytosis with a raised protein and a normal glucose is a viral pattern. With a positive HSV-1 PCR this confirms herpes simplex encephalitis. Red cells that do not clear between tubes fit the haemorrhagic temporal lobe inflammation. A normal glucose, no organisms and a negative cryptococcal antigen make bacterial and cryptococcal infection unlikely, but Listeria can also give a lymphocytic CSF and the culture is pending.
  • Changes: continue IV aciclovir for a full course (at least 14 days, 21 days in an immunosuppressed patient, guided by ID; repeat CSF PCR before stopping if advised). Stop empirical antibiotics only on infectious diseases advice once the culture is negative. An early negative PCR would not have excluded HSV.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Jane Foweler, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Jane now, here in the emergency department, including what you want the nurses to escalate to you.
Jane's partner, Sam, has just arrived. Please explain to Sam what is wrong with Jane, and what to watch for and the follow-up once she eventually goes home.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED junior doctor; Jane Foweler, 68.
  • Situation: herpes simplex encephalitis confirmed on CSF PCR; GCS fell from 14 to 12 at 19:30, meeting rapid response criteria.
  • Background: one day of progressive fever, confusion, personality change, right arm weakness and paraesthesia, and vomiting twice; previous cold sores; rheumatoid arthritis on weekly methotrexate and intermittent prednisolone (immunosuppressed); no known drug allergies.
  • Assessment: T 39.2, RR 26, HR 114; GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5), right arm 4/5. Bloods: no metabolic cause, lymphopenia, CRP 24, normal coagulation and creatinine. CT: no mass or haemorrhage, subtle left temporal hypodensity. CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis 110, protein 0.95, normal glucose ratio (0.60), HSV-1 PCR detected.
  • Recommendation: I have activated a rapid response call for the GCS fall; please attend now; ICU review; continue aciclovir 680 mg IV 8-hourly (first dose 14:10); admit under neurology and ID; MRI and EEG.

Herpes simplex encephalitis: fever with one day of worsening confusion, personality change and a right arm deficit; previous cold sores; immunosuppressed; left temporal hypodensity on CT; lymphocytic CSF with raised protein, normal glucose and HSV-1 PCR detected.

  • Bacterial meningitis, including Listeria: for: fever, confusion, age and methotrexate; against: no headache, neck stiffness, photophobia or rash, normal CSF glucose, no organisms; culture pending.
  • Brain abscess: for: fever, focal deficit, immunosuppressed; against: no swinging fevers or seizures, no mass on CT.
  • Ischaemic stroke: for: age, right arm weakness; against: fever, progressive course, no facial droop or dysarthria, inflammatory CSF.
  • Delirium from another cause: for: acute confusion, 4AT 7; against: normal metabolic screen and urine, focal signs, positive CSF.

1. DRSABCD: rapid response or senior to the bedside now for the GCS fall; ICU review; GCS and pupils every 15 minutes until stable (then at least hourly); BGL; airway protection if GCS 8 or less (bonus).
  2. Aciclovir 680 mg (10 mg/kg) IV 8-hourly (correctly started on suspicion at 14:10, before CT and LP), next dose 22:10 on time, no renal reduction (CrCl ~70), hydrate, monitor creatinine; at least 14 days, 21 days as she is immunosuppressed, guided by ID.
  3. Continue the ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin given from 14:05 (Listeria cover) until the CSF culture is negative, on ID advice.
  4. Deterioration, seizures and ICP: urgent repeat CT brain (or urgent MRI if immediately available) for oedema, haemorrhage or mass effect, and urgent EEG for non-convulsive status; benzodiazepine then levetiracetam for seizures; head up; ICU.
  5. Admit under neurology with ID; MRI brain with gadolinium.
  6. Withhold methotrexate (rheumatology to plan restart).
  7. Nurse escalation triggers (at least four): must include any further fall in GCS, a seizure and unequal pupils; others: new weakness or speech change, new headache or vomiting, falling urine output or rising creatinine on aciclovir.

• Now: she has become drowsier in the last hour; a specialist team is with her, she may need to move to intensive care, and we will keep you updated.
  • Plain words: an infection and swelling of the brain caused by the cold sore virus waking up, more likely because her arthritis medicines lower her immunity. It is treated with an antiviral drip for 2 to 3 weeks.
  • Catching: the brain infection is not passed on; the cold sore virus is very common; usual hygiene.
  • Recovery: early treatment helps, but recovery is often slow and memory, mood or behaviour problems can last; answered honestly.
  • At home: call 000 for a seizure or if she is hard to wake; come back to the ED for a returning fever, more confusion or new weakness, or for new behaviour change, abnormal movements or seizures in the weeks after discharge (relapse or autoimmune encephalitis).
  • Follow-up: neurology follow-up with cognitive assessment and rehabilitation.

ddx.for: One day of fever with worsening confusion, personality change and right arm weakness in an immunosuppressed woman with past cold sores, left temporal hypodensity on CT and HSV-1 PCR detected in a lymphocytic CSF.
ddx.against: Headache and seizures are common but absent here; their absence is less informative in an immunosuppressed patient.

ddx.for: She has fever and confusion, is 68 and takes methotrexate and intermittent prednisolone, which puts her at risk of Listeria.
ddx.against: She has no headache, neck stiffness, photophobia or rash, and her CSF has a normal glucose, no organisms and a lymphocytic pattern.

ddx.for: She has fever and a focal right arm deficit and is immunosuppressed.
ddx.against: She has no swinging fevers, seizures or ear, sinus or dental source, and CT shows no mass or collection.

ddx.for: She is 68 and has right arm weakness with sensory loss.
ddx.against: She has fever and a progressive course over a day, no facial droop or dysarthria, an inflammatory CSF and a CT change outside a single arterial territory.

ddx.dx: Delirium from another cause (sepsis, urinary infection, drugs or metabolic)
ddx.for: She has acute confusion with fever, an acute change reported by her partner, and a 4AT of 7.
ddx.against: Her sodium, glucose, calcium, renal and liver function and urine dipstick are normal, she has focal signs, and her CSF is positive for HSV-1.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner also plays the nurse. Give the observations and BGL when asked, relay Sam's collateral history from the paramedic handover if the candidate asks for it, and give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Give the examination findings as a block as soon as the candidate names each system; do not wait for the manoeuvres to be performed in full. The patient answers slowly and loses the thread of long or multi-part questions. If the candidate asks for blood, CT or CSF results, say they will be given in Part 2. If the candidate orders aciclovir, cultures or a CT in Part 1, credit it under the matching Management item when they repeat it in Part 2. Item 32.1 (aciclovir starts on suspicion) is credited if it is said in Part 1 or in the answer to question 3. The cold sores are given only if asked.

In Part 2, read the lead (including the medication chart: antibiotics at 14:05, aciclovir at 14:10, benzylpenicillin repeated at 18:05), hand over all four results together, then ask the questions in order. For the fourth question, the student playing Jane plays her partner, Sam, and asks the questions in the Part 2 script.

A high-performing candidate takes a structured history that screens the four main differentials (meningitis, stroke, abscess, delirium), finds the right arm symptoms, the immunosuppression and the cold sores, and seeks collateral. They examine conscious state by GCS component and with a 4AT, look for meningism and papilloedema, and find the right arm signs. In Part 2 they recognise the GCS fall as a rapid response trigger, read the CSF as viral with HSV-1 confirmed, and know that CT came before LP because of the focal deficit, reduced GCS and immunosuppression. They state that aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly (680 mg) should start on suspicion and continue it, cover bacterial meningitis with Listeria until excluded, involve ICU, neurology and ID, withhold methotrexate, set clear triggers for the nurses, and explain the illness to Sam honestly.

A borderline candidate asks a list of questions without structure, misses the immunosuppression or the focal symptoms, or does not examine conscious state formally. They call the CSF "abnormal" without a pattern, say they would wait for the PCR before starting aciclovir, cannot give the dose, or do not escalate the falling GCS.
explain:
Diagnosis: herpes simplex encephalitis

Fever plus an altered mental state (confusion, personality or behaviour change, reduced conscious level), with or without focal signs or seizures, is encephalitis until proven otherwise. Jane has a one-day progressive illness with fever, confusion, slowed thinking, personality change noticed by her partner, and a right arm motor and sensory deficit with word-finding pauses, which lateralises to the left hemisphere. The left temporal change on CT fits the word-finding pauses, but the anteromedial temporal lobe contains no motor or sensory cortex, so the right arm corticospinal and sensory signs imply involvement beyond the area seen on CT (for example insular or frontoparietal spread, or surrounding oedema), which CT underestimates and MRI defines better. Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) is the commonest cause of sporadic encephalitis. It has a predilection for the temporal and inferior frontal lobes, which explains the behavioural change and memory and language problems. Jane's previous cold sores and her immunosuppression (weekly methotrexate and repeated prednisolone) add weight. Immunosuppressed patients may present atypically, and the absence of headache here does not argue against it.

Differentials and how the history separates them

  • Bacterial meningitis: headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and a rash (meningococcal). At 68 and immunosuppressed, Jane is at risk of Listeria, which can cause rhombencephalitis and a lymphocytic CSF.
  • Stroke: sudden onset, facial droop, dysarthria and a vascular territory deficit; palpitations raise atrial fibrillation as a source. Fever and a progressive course make it unlikely.
  • Brain abscess: fever, focal deficit, seizures, swinging fevers and a source (ears, sinuses, teeth, endocarditis); a ring-enhancing lesion on contrast imaging.
  • Delirium: an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition caused by something else (infection, drugs, alcohol withdrawal, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, dehydration, urinary retention, constipation). Delirium is a syndrome with a cause to be found, not a final diagnosis. The 4AT is a quick screen: a score of 4 or more suggests delirium.

Conscious state

The GCS is scored by component and best response: eyes 4, verbal 5, motor 6 (total 3 to 15). Always report the components (here E4 V4 M6, then E3 V4 M5) and compare with the patient's baseline. If there is no response to voice, apply a standard physical stimulus: fingertip pressure for eye opening and flexion, and trapezius pinch or supraorbital pressure to test for localising. Under the NSW Between the Flags criteria, a fall in GCS of 2 or more points is a rapid response call. Consider airway protection and intubation when the GCS is 8 or less, depending on the cause and the expected course.

Investigations

CT before LP is indicated when there is a focal neurological deficit, reduced conscious level, a new seizure, papilloedema or immunocompromise, because these raise the risk of a mass lesion and herniation. Jane meets three of these. Imaging must never delay empirical treatment. CT is often normal early in HSV encephalitis. MRI is far more sensitive, showing temporal lobe and insular T2/FLAIR change, and EEG may show temporal slowing or periodic discharges and detects non-convulsive seizures.

CSFBacterialViral (including HSV)TB or fungal

Jane's CSF is the viral pattern (CSF:plasma glucose 3.7/6.2 = 0.60, normal), with red cells reflecting the haemorrhagic, necrotising nature of HSV encephalitis. CSF HSV PCR is the diagnostic test. It can be falsely negative in the first days, so a negative early PCR in a suggestive case means continuing aciclovir and repeating the LP, not stopping treatment.

Management (eTG)

  • Resuscitate and escalate: DRSABCD, a rapid response for the falling GCS, ICU review, GCS and pupils every 15 minutes until stable (then at least hourly), and airway protection if needed.
  • Aciclovir: 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly, started as soon as encephalitis is suspected, without waiting for imaging, LP or PCR, because delay worsens outcome. Adjust for renal function, keep the patient well hydrated and monitor creatinine (crystal nephropathy). Treat for at least 14 days, 21 days in an immunosuppressed patient, guided by infectious diseases (repeat CSF PCR before stopping if advised).
  • Until bacterial meningitis is excluded: in older or immunosuppressed adults, empirical ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV 4-hourly for Listeria (eTG; amoxicillin/ampicillin 2 g IV 4-hourly is an alternative), continued until the CSF culture is negative, on infectious diseases advice. eTG recommends dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly before or with the first antibiotic dose when bacterial meningitis is suspected. Here the picture was encephalitic without meningism, so the treating team judged not to give it; this is a reasonable judgement but not mandatory. If it had been started, it would be stopped once the CSF showed a viral pattern with HSV detected. Dexamethasone is not a treatment for HSV encephalitis.
  • Complications: a falling GCS with new tachypnoea and a rising heart rate and BP calls for an urgent repeat CT brain (or urgent MRI if immediately available) for oedema, haemorrhage or mass effect, and an urgent EEG for non-convulsive status. Treat seizures (a benzodiazepine first, then a second-line agent such as levetiracetam). For raised intracranial pressure: head up 30 to 45 degrees, osmotherapy and ICU and neurosurgical input.
  • Supportive care: fluids, antipyretics, a swallow screen, VTE prophylaxis, and delirium care with family present.
  • Immunosuppression: withhold methotrexate and plan its restart with rheumatology. Repeated prednisolone courses raise the possibility of adrenal suppression, so check when she last took it and consider stress-dose steroid cover.
  • Disposition: admit under neurology with infectious diseases, or to ICU if the GCS keeps falling.

Safety netting and follow-up

In hospital, nurses escalate a further fall in GCS, seizures, new focal signs, unequal pupils, headache or vomiting, and falling urine output or rising creatinine. After discharge, the family calls 000 for a seizure or if she is hard to wake, and returns to the ED for returning fever, worsening confusion or new weakness. They also return for new behaviour change, abnormal movements or seizures in the weeks after discharge: relapse or autoimmune (NMDA-receptor) encephalitis follows HSV encephalitis in up to about a quarter of patients, typically 2 to 8 weeks later. Many survivors have lasting memory, behavioural or language problems, so follow-up includes neurology, cognitive and neuropsychological assessment, rehabilitation, a driving review under Austroads standards, rheumatology before methotrexate restarts, the GP, and support for her partner.
points: Fever with an altered mental state, personality change or focal signs is encephalitis until proven otherwise. Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly at once, without waiting for CT, LP or PCR.
Immunosuppression (methotrexate, corticosteroids) blunts the presentation and widens the differential: cover bacterial meningitis, including Listeria, until the CSF excludes it.
CT comes before LP when there is a focal deficit, reduced GCS, immunocompromise, a new seizure or papilloedema, but imaging must never delay treatment.
HSV encephalitis gives a lymphocytic CSF with raised protein, normal glucose and often red cells. HSV PCR confirms it, but an early negative PCR does not exclude it.

Report the GCS by component. If there is no response to voice, apply a standard physical stimulus: fingertip pressure for eye opening and flexion, and trapezius pinch or supraorbital pressure to test for localising. Treat a fall of 2 or more points as a rapid response call, and consider airway protection at GCS 8 or less.
Delirium is a syndrome, not a diagnosis: screen with the 4AT, take a collateral history, and look for the cause.
